img-p012-2.saw: Figure 1 infographic mapping seven planning phases to WHO/partner tools, with this Reference Architecture placed beside them
img-p012-2.draft: Figure 1, 'The Reference Architecture within planning and implementing a digital health enterprise' (Executive Summary). The infographic lists seven phases down the left, each with its steps: 01 Assessing the current state and enabling environment; 02 Establishing a shared understanding and strategic planning; 03 Defining the future state; 04 Planning the enterprise architecture; 05 Determining health content requirements; 06 M&E of digital health implementations and fostering data use; 07 Implementing, maintaining and scaling. Beside each phase are tiles for supporting resources, marked as PDF or online, such as the WHO-ITU National eHealth Strategy Toolkit, the Digital Implementation Investment Guide (DIIG), the WHO classification of digital health interventions, Open Health Information Exchange (OpenHIE), TOGAF, the Global Digital Health Certification Network, WHO SMART Guidelines (digital adaptation kits and machine-readable recommendations) and WHO FIC, ICD-11, HL7 FHIR and LOINC. A dashed box at the far right, labelled 'WHO-ITU Reference Architecture for DPI-H', sits level with Phases 01 to 04. A footer expands the abbreviations HIS, ICT, ITU, M&E and SDG.

img-p041-2.saw: Figure 2.2 infographic of REDDHI: purpose, why resilient/essential, STAC foundations, role, objectives, principles
img-p041-2.draft: Figure 2.2, 'REDDHI: resilient and essential dimensions, the full-STAC foundations, and REDDHI's role within national digital architecture' (section 2.2, Resilient Essential Data and Digital Health Infrastructure). Headed 'Resilient Essential Data & Digital Health Infrastructure', it describes REDDHI as a direction of travel rather than a fixed destination. It explains 'Why resilient' (survives funding volatility, reduces external vendor dependency, long-term technical sustainability, builds local capacity) and 'Why essential' (minimum capabilities, a foundation for multiple use cases, investment efficiency, a subset of the broader national architecture). A band 'Built on open full-STAC foundations' has four parts: Standards (HL7 FHIR, ICD, SNOMED CT, LOINC, CQL), Technologies (open-source tooling and SDKs), Architectures (DPI-based, modular, plug-and-play) and Content (WHO SMART Guidelines). Further bands give REDDHI's role (a subset of the whole, connected to foundational DPI, governed for interoperability), five objectives (transition from fragmentation, build governed and interoperable foundations, enable local and regional innovation, ensure technical and financial sustainability, position countries for large-scale investment) and nine guiding principles.

img-p048-2.saw: Figure 2.3 semicircular diagram of the ten DPI-H architecture design principles with icons and definitions
img-p048-2.draft: Figure 2.3, 'DPI-H Architecture Design Principles' (section 2.3). A semicircle of ten blue segments, each with an icon, surrounds the central title. Each principle has a one-line definition: Governance, Open Standards, Interoperability, Sustainability, Modularity, Local Capacity, Equity and Inclusion, Data Ownership, Access and Control, Trust and Security, and Ethics. For example, Modularity is 'building loosely coupled components that can be introduced, replaced, and improved incrementally', and Interoperability is 'designing for meaningful data exchange across systems and foundational DPI from the outset'.

img-p056-2.saw: Figure 3.1 ArchiMate chain of four elements linked by 'realises', each annotated with a Client Registry example
img-p056-2.draft: Figure 3.1, 'Realisation relationships among architectural elements' (section 3.1). Four ArchiMate elements are stacked vertically and joined by dotted 'realises' arrows that point upward: Application Component realises Application Function, which realises Application Service, which realises Business Capability. img-p059-2.saw: Figure 3.2 full layered integrated view of the DPI-H reference architecture, goals through technology, with an interoperability column
img-p059-2.draft: Figure 3.2, the DPI-H reference architecture as a layered integrated view (section 3.3, The reference architecture in practice). Top to bottom: Strategic Health Goals G1 to G7 (Trusted data foundations, Health workforce, Quality and continuity of care, Personal health record, Supply chain, Health financing, Climate and epidemic resilience); a Cross-cutting Governance band (Policy, legislation and regulation; Cybersecurity, privacy and consent; Standards, certification and conformance; Semantic governance and stewardship; Auditability, assurance and accountability); Stakeholders, such as citizens, health workforce, government/MoH, facilities, financial entities, suppliers, development agencies and research; and Capabilities, such as identity management, access/consent/trust, health record management, knowledge management, clinical services and care coordination, health workforce management, health financing, supply chain, analytics and BI, and climate and public-health surveillance. Next is the Point-of-Service and Functional Applications layer, which the private sector, donors, NGOs and implementers build: provider systems, case management, pharmacy, CHW and community, citizen/patient apps, supply chain, health coverage and claims, financing and workforce operations, and public health apps. These consume the DPI-H layer through standards-based APIs. The DPI-H layer, government-stewarded reusable infrastructure, holds Reusable Components (Clinical services with a Computable Decision Support Engine, Supply chain with a Supplier Registry, Health financing with a Benefits Package Registry, Public health and analytics with a PH Surveillance Platform and HMIS, AI-enabled intelligence, and Secondary use). It also holds a Shared Data Layer of core registries, several starred as REDDHI components: Client Registry, Lifelong Health Record, Health Workforce Registry, Facility Registry, Product Registry, Terminology Service and Logical Information Model Repository. Below these come the Foundational DPI Layer (DPI-F: foundational identity, national trust services, payment rails, data exchange fabric, CRVS and other sectors, geo-location and notification) and the Technology Layer (hybrid/sovereign cloud, AI/ML platform, security and trust operations, data platform, observability/DevSecOps). A cross-cutting Interoperability column on the right holds an Information Mediator (API gateway, HIE), open standards (such as HL7 FHIR, IHE, openEHR, IPS, SNOMED CT, ICD-11, LOINC, GS1, CDS Hooks, SMART on FHIR, OpenID/OAuth2, DICOM) and integration patterns (REST APIs, event streams, IHE documents, federated query, bulk data, cross-border IHR/IPS). It connects to each layer through interface markers.

img-p061-2.saw: Figure 3.3 ArchiMate goal-to-component view for the Trusted Personal Health Record goal
img-p061-2.draft: Figure 3.3, 'Simplified view of a single health goal (Establish Trusted Personal Health Records)' (section 3.3). At the top, a 'TPHR Goals' group holds the overall goal of a secure, universally accessible system for issuing verifiable digital health records. It is composed of four sub-goals: a verifiable health record for every individual; patient control and consent-based sharing; trust, security and privacy in all transactions; and interoperability across providers, facilities and jurisdictions. A 'TPHR Outcomes' group lists four outcomes, such as citizens empowered to own, access and share their health records. These realise the goals. A 'TPHR Implementation' area shows capabilities realising those outcomes, including Health Record Management, Identity and Authentication, Universal Access Enablement, Dynamic Consent Management, Data Governance, Data Sharing and Authorization, Audit and Compliance Monitoring, Trust and Verification, Data Privacy, Incident Detection and Response, Interoperability and Health Information Exchange, Terminology and Data Management, and Provider and Facility Verification. Below them, application services such as Client Identity Service, Consent Management Service, FHIR API Service and Terminology Service (SNOMED, ICD, LOINC) are realised by application components such as Lifelong Health Record, Client Registry, PHR Portal/Mobile App, PKI/Trust Infrastructure, IAM/Access Control System, SIEM, Interoperability Middleware, Terminology Service and Facility Registry.

img-p062-2.saw: Figure 3.4 ArchiMate layered view of one TPHR sub-goal down to metadata registry components
img-p062-2.draft: Figure 3.4, 'Layered view for one sub-goal relating to Establish Trusted Personal Health Records' (section 3.3). The sub-goal 'Establish a secure, universally accessible, verifiable health record for every individual' is realised by the outcome 'Population has verifiable digital health records'. Within 'TPHR Sub-goal #1 Implementation', three capabilities realise that outcome: Health Record Management, Identity and Authentication, and Universal Access Enablement. These are realised by the product 'Trusted Personal Health Record (PHR)', which three services serve: Health Record Management Service, Client Identity Service and Record Verification Service. In turn these are realised by the components Lifelong Health Record, Client Registry and PKI/Trust Infrastructure. A 'Metadata Components' group at the bottom holds the Client Registry, Facility Registry, Health Worker Registry, Product Registry and Terminology Service.

img-p063-2.saw: ArchiMate layered view of the Quality and Continuity of Care needs-assessment sub-goal, captioned Figure 3.5
img-p063-2.draft: Figure 3.5 on page 52, 'Layered view for one sub-goal relating to ensuring Quality and Continuity of Care' (section 3.3). The sub-goal 'Comprehensive Needs Assessment' (systematic evaluation of a patient's complete health status, risks and care requirements) is realised by the outcome 'Integrated, Person-Centered Care'. In 'Q&CC Sub-goal #1 Implementation', five capabilities realise that outcome: Care Protocol Management, Task-Sharing Orchestration, Patient History Integration, Quality and Performance Monitoring, and Decision Support. These are realised by the product 'Integrated Shared Care Plan (SCP)', which four services serve: Care Protocol Management, Clinical Decision Support, Patient History Aggregation Service, and Care Coordination and Task. Those services are realised by or served from the components Knowledge Base Engine, Electronic Medical Record, Interoperability Layer, Access Control and Authentication, Lifelong Health Record and Client Registry. A 'Grouping' at the bottom, which these components access, holds the Client Registry, Health Worker Registry, Facility Registry, Terminology Server and Product Registry.

img-p070-2.saw: Figure 3.4.1 three-layer diagram of Semantic Governance Infrastructure and content flow
img-p070-2.draft: Figure 3.4.1, 'Semantic Governance Infrastructure: the governance, runtime, and content-and-application layers, and the flow of content between them' (section 3.4.5). Three horizontal layers are separated by dashed lines. Governance Services contains LIMR, Profile authoring, Conformance resources and Governance TMS. Runtime Services contains Runtime TS and a placeholder box. Content and Application Layers contains a row of IGs (IG 1, IG 2, IG 3 and more) and a row of Applications/Use Cases (App 1, App 2, App 3 and more). An arrow labelled 'Content syndication' runs from Global Content Sources, outside the layers, into Governance TMS, and a two-way arrow links Governance TMS with Runtime TS.

img-p072-2.saw: Figure 3.4.2 terminology services maturity model chart, from Nascent to Data Exchange
img-p072-2.draft: Figure 3.4.2, 'A terminology maturity spectrum, from minimal reference-list management to a fully governed, multi-stakeholder ecosystem', adapted from the OpenHIE Terminology Service maturity model (section 3.4.5). A rising line plots five maturity levels: Nascent (no centrally defined content or governance); Emerging (some centrally defined content in non-standard formats, with limited adoption and governance); Shared Electronic Reference (up-to-date definitions aligned across key programmes); Digital Subscription (key systems subscribe electronically to the central service to stay up to date); and Data Exchange (the terminology service automates information exchange, for example code validation and value set expansion). Red break marks between Emerging and Shared Electronic Reference show a steep climb. A callout notes that many LMICs are at early stages and that this step needs a different way of doing business. Braces underneath group the first three levels as emphasising selection, definition and governance of standards, and the last two as emphasising use of terminologies for data exchange.

img-p073-2.saw: Figure 3.4.3 NHDD stacked-layer diagram of hierarchical terminology content with top-down and feedback arrows
img-p073-2.draft: Figure 3.4.3, 'Hierarchical terminology content, from global reference standards to facility-level dictionaries, with top-down customisation and upward feedback', adapted from the OpenHIE National Health Data Dictionary (NHDD) framework (section 3.4.5). Titled 'NHDD Framework: Content Structure', it stacks five layers from top to bottom: Reference/Administrative Code Sets (for example SNOMED, ICD, HL7); Curated Concept Sources/Interface Terminologies (for example CIEL, IMO); Country-level Subsets/Customizations; Organization-level Dictionaries/Customizations; and Facility-level Dictionaries (for example formularies). A downward arrow on the left says that international standards are selected and customised for country use, then adapted further for local implementation. An upward arrow on the right reads 'Submissions / Feedback to Standards' and 'Responsive Local & National Governance'.

img-p077-2.saw: layered DPI-H integrated view (applications, DPI-H, DPI-F, interoperability column), captioned Figure 3.5 in section 3.5.3
img-p077-2.draft: Figure 3.5 on page 66, the DPI-H reference architecture layered view (section 3.5.3, How the components are organised). It is a reduced form of the integrated view in Figure 3.2 without the goals, governance, stakeholder, capability and technology bands. Titled 'DPI-H Reference Architecture: government-stewarded reusable Digital Public Infrastructure for Health', it shows the Point-of-Service and Functional Applications layer on top, consuming the DPI-H layer through standards-based APIs. The DPI-H layer has Reusable Components (Clinical services with a Computable Decision Support Engine, Supply chain with a Supplier Registry, Health financing with a Benefits Package Registry, Public health and analytics with a PH Surveillance Platform and HMIS, AI-enabled intelligence, and Secondary use) and a Shared Data Layer (Client Registry, Lifelong Health Record, Health Workforce Registry, Facility Registry, Product Registry, Terminology Service, Logical Information Model Repository; the first five are starred as REDDHI components). Beneath is the Foundational DPI Layer (DPI-F): foundational identity, national trust services, payment rails, data exchange fabric, CRVS and other sectors, and geo-location and notification. A cross-cutting Interoperability column on the right holds the Information Mediator (API gateway, HIE), open standards and integration patterns.

img-p087-2.saw: Figure 3.6 five small network diagrams of alternative data-exchange patterns
img-p087-2.draft: Figure 3.6, 'Exchange patterns that can coexist within a single country' (section 3.6.3). Five panels show the same kind of systems connected in different ways. Direct connections: systems A to D linked point-to-point. Central service bus: five systems all attached to one orange service bus. Gateways: systems A, B and C, each behind its own gateway, with the gateways linked. Distributed access points: systems A, B and C, each with an access point (AP); the APs are linked by solid data lines, while dashed lines join each one to a central 'Registry & oversight' box that carries no data. Publish–subscribe (asynchronous): System A publishes to an event broker, which notifies systems B, C and D. The page text states that the architecture does not prescribe one pattern.

img-p093-2.saw: Figure 3.7.1 ArchiMate diagram of systems realising IHE actors around the ITI-41 transaction
img-p093-2.draft: Figure 3.7.1 (section 3.7.2, The model), showing a system realising an actor with its offered and required services, and two actors connected by a transaction. The components Document Source and Document Repository are both assigned to the interaction 'Provide and Register Document Set [ITI-41]'. 'Vendor EHR Product' realises Document Source, and 'Vendor 2 EHR product' realises Document Repository; both links are drawn as red dotted lines. Document Repository realises the service 'Register Document Set', which serves Document Source.

img-p094-2.saw: Figure 3.7.2 ArchiMate conformance-testing view with System Under Test, Simulator and Test Operator
img-p094-2.draft: Figure 3.7.2, 'Conformance testing view' (section 3.7.2). The System Under Test, which contains a 'Document Capture UI' interface, realises the Document Source actor. A Simulator realises the opposite Document Repository actor. Both actors are assigned to the interaction 'Provide and Register Document Set [ITI-41]'. The Document Capture UI serves a Test Operator role, which is assigned to the process 'Create and submit document' that triggers the same ITI-41 interaction. This shows that the system can also be tested end to end through its user interface.

img-p254-2.saw: Figure A.1 flow of five semantic-governance capabilities with linked roles and supporting tools, with legend
img-p254-2.draft: Figure A.1, 'Semantic governance capabilities, the roles that carry them out, and the supporting application components' (Appendix F, Semantic Governance Infrastructure: capability details). Five capabilities run left to right as a flow: Consume, Change requests, Change management, Publication and Monitoring. The step from Change management to Publication is drawn dashed. Roles and information objects are attached above: Stakeholder to Consume; Author and Owner to Change management; Content and Upstream content to Publication; and Management rules to Monitoring. Supporting tools are attached below: Change-request tooling to Change requests, Authoring to Change management, and Repository to Publication. A legend distinguishes the three types: capability, role or information object, and supporting tool.
